newsitem.title: USA: CME hogs and pork bellies end mixed, mostly higher.
newsitem.headline: CME hogs and pork bellies end mixed, mostly higher.

text.p: CME hog futures traded mixed late on rolling of long positions from December into back months but nearby months firmed on stronger-than-expected cash markets, traders said. Pork bellies rallied on stronger cash belly quotes and evening of positions ahead of the CME out-of-town belly report, traders said.

Firm cash hog prices offset rolling of longs out of December, sources said. Projections last week of weak cash hog prices this week failed to materialize as marketings remained light and packers boosted bids, traders said.
The cash pork complex also showed a better-than-anticipated tone ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, sources noted.
Although ham prices were weakening seasonally, loins and belly prices advanced, prompting ideas of firmer cash hog prices Wednesday.
Hog futures closed 1.100 cent a lb higher to 0.075 lower with April pacing the advance at a one-month high on spreading while December finished 0.375 at 59.050 cents.
Rand Financials bought December at its early low, traders said. Rosenthal Collins and local short covering turned December up despite the spreading.
Refco spread long February/short December early and Rosenthal did the spread late. Other spreaders bought April and sold December, pit sources said.
In hog options, commission houses sold calls and bought puts, pit sources added.

Pork bellies rallied again late after mixed selling took prices down after initial buy stops were hit. Firmer-than-expected cash belly prices quoted by USDA at noon and continued talk of light storings prompted commercial demand, traders said.
Cash belly prices were quoted steady to $1.00 higher by USDA in its midday carlot pork report.
Pork belly futures closed up 0.700 cent to off 0.025 with February up most at 77.400 cents per lb.

Belly futures were also seen higher Wednesday, buoyed by the CME out-of-town report which showed net storings in warehouses outside Chicago last week at 838,000 lbs, well under the range of analyst estimates, traders said. Expectations had been for a net increase of 2.5 million to 3.0 million lbs in. Year-ago storings the same week were 4.460 million lbs. The less-than-expected storings were attributed to increased demand, but much of the difference from last year was a result of the week that Thanksgiving falls into and slaughter rates those weeks.

"A year ago Saturday (packers) killed 250,000 hogs whereas a week ago this year, they only killed about 30,000 or 40,000, so on that (year ago) Saturday we (produced) about six million more pounds of bellies," said Rich Tokheim, President of Investment Research Co.
